design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis, reported to PRISMA, of human studies published January 2004 to February 2015 that gave neuropsychological or cognitive tasks either after acute administration of cannabis or cannabinoids (THC intravenously, orally, smoked or vaporised; nabilone; dronabinol; cannabis differing in CBD content) or to people with regular or former cannabis use. PubMed and Scopus; titles screened (6,241 records), 356 full texts, 105 studies included. Qualitative synthesis by cognitive domain, separately for acute, chronic and abstinence evidence, with strength-of-evidence ratings from +++ to - agreed by the authors (Table 1) and a list of key findings (Table 2). Version read: the Author's Accepted Manuscript (27 PDF pages), not the version of record; the search strategy, extraction methods and per-study data are in Supplements 1 and 2, which are not on file.
can_establish: Which cognitive domains the 2004-2015 literature on task performance most often reports as impaired during intoxication, in people who use cannabis regularly and after abstinence, as judged by the authors, and how few studies (18, mostly at 3 to 5 weeks of abstinence) addressed persistence or recovery.
cannot_establish: The size of any impairment (nothing is pooled and no effect sizes are given in the main text); whether differences in people who use cannabis regularly were caused by cannabis rather than by pre-existing differences or other drug use (mostly cross-sectional studies, more than half without IQ or education data, no study-level risk-of-bias assessment); or whether deficits persist after long abstinence.

sample.recruitment: Search of PubMed and Scopus for studies published January 2004 to February 2015 (Abstract, AM p. 2; Figure 1, AM p. 27); the strategy is in Supplement 1 (not read). The included samples, as the text describes them, are laboratory volunteers with infrequent or regular use given cannabinoids; adolescents and young adults, including college students; older adults (about 35-51); adolescents and adults in treatment or pharmacotherapy trials; twins discordant for use; and community cohorts followed for years.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: neuropsychological or cognitive experimental tasks given to people with regular or former cannabis use or after acute administration of cannabis or synthetic or plant cannabinoids; cannabis the primary drug of interest; human participants. Excluded: studies in which cannabis was not the primary drug of concern; questionnaire (trait) measures of cognition; samples with major psychopathology or neurological conditions; animal research; neuroimaging, electrophysiological or autonomic measures as primary outcomes; treatment as the primary focus; real-world multiplex tasks such as driving; case studies (Figure 1 legend, AM p. 23). No comparator is specified.
sample.demographics: Not given per study in the main text (Supplement 2, Table S1, not read). About 75% of studies had predominantly male samples; gender effects were tested in about 12% and very few were found (AM p. 8).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition in the prospective studies is not reported in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases; a first screen on titles only; a window of January 2004 to February 2015 with no stated reason for leaving out earlier studies (the earlier literature enters only through earlier reviews, refs 18-22, four of them by the senior author, and a few earlier studies cited as previous findings); language limits not stated in the main text; no reference-list, registry, grey-literature or expert searching reported. Questionnaire measures, imaging or electrophysiological outcomes, real-world tasks such as driving and samples with major psychopathology were excluded, so the review concerns laboratory task performance only. Two included studies are by the senior author (Solowij et al., 2011, ref. 47; Solowij et al., 2012, ref. 124).

exposure.measurement: As in the included studies: acute administration in the laboratory (THC intravenously, orally, smoked or vaporised; nabilone; dronabinol; cannabis of differing CBD content, including naturalistic studies of people smoking their own cannabis), or self-reported histories of regular or former use, from which the reviewers extracted age of onset, duration, frequency and quantity of use and the period of abstinence before testing (Method, AM p. 4). Some studies measured cannabinoids in hair (THC to CBD ratios). How abstinence was verified is not summarised in the main text.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Doses of the acute studies are in Supplements 1 and 2 (not read). The Discussion notes that intravenous, smoked and vaporised cannabinoids act sooner and for a shorter time than oral or sublingual ones, and that most acute studies tested once, immediately or within two to three hours of dosing (AM p. 8). For chronic studies the extent of exposure is heterogeneous and not standardised; the review sets no minimum definition of regular use.
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use are common, and a disconcerting number of studies failed to report or account for them; studies handled them by heterogeneous, often poorly specified exclusion criteria, by matching or by covariates with different metrics. The authors state that the impairing effects of chronic use mostly held after controlling for other substance use, but not in all studies (details in Supplement 1, not read) (AM p. 9).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Chronic studies: not summarised. Abstinence studies: more than 24 hours, most often 21-35 days, few longer; 7 days to over 1 year in the cross-sectional studies and 21 days to 4-8 years in the prospective ones (AM p. 10).

comparison.controls: Acute studies: placebo or baseline conditions within single samples (23 studies of people without regular use, 11 of people with regular use); only 4 compared groups (2 people who use cannabis against controls, 2 frequent against infrequent use). Chronic and abstinence studies: people who do not use cannabis, in some studies people who drink alcohol or co-twins; also within-group associations with use metrics.
comparison.matching: Varies by study; more than 50% of studies did not report IQ or years of education (AM p. 9).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Ability measured before first use in only two of the prospective abstinence studies (Fried et al., 2005; Meier et al., 2012); a substantial number of studies did not control for premorbid functioning or assess current intellectual functioning (AM pp. 9-10).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Often not reported or not accounted for (AM p. 9).

outcomes.instruments: Neuropsychological tasks, grouped by domain: verbal learning and memory (word-list learning with immediate and delayed recall and recognition); working memory (Sternberg, delayed matching to sample, spatial and numeric tasks, n-back, digit recall and digit span, letter-number sequencing, spatial span, WAIS working-memory tasks); attention (focused, divided and sustained attention, processing speed, rapid visual information processing, visual search, tracking, trail making, paced serial addition); attentional bias to cannabis cues; psychomotor function (finger tapping, critical tracking, choice reaction time, digit-symbol substitution); executive function (planning, reasoning, interference control, problem solving, Block Design, Go/No-Go and stop-signal inhibition, verbal fluency, time estimation); decision making (Iowa Gambling Task, delay discounting, behavioural risk-taking tasks).
outcomes.validity_norms: The validity of tasks is not appraised; the authors attribute mixed findings partly to the wide range of tasks used (AM pp. 5, 8, 11).
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment is a group difference in task performance (against placebo, controls or baseline) or an association of poorer performance with cannabis-use metrics. Strength of evidence is rated per domain from +++ (strong and largely consistent evidence for impairment) through ++ (moderate), + (weak, few studies) and +- (mixed) to - (little or none), weighed subjectively on the number and quality (design, sample size) of studies and agreed by the authors (Table 1 and footnote, AM pp. 24-25).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis). The count is the 11 domain rows of Table 1, each rated for acute, chronic and abstinence evidence (33 ratings).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Who screened and who extracted is not stated in the main text (Supplement 1, not read).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. No pooled or study-level effect sizes are given in the main text; per-study findings are tabulated in Supplement 2, Table S1 (not read). Evidence is summarised as numbers of studies and qualitative ratings per domain (Table 1) and as key-finding bullets (Table 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA is cited as the reporting guideline (Method, AM p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: No rule is given for turning the number, quality and direction of studies into a rating beyond the footnote describing a subjective consensus; Table 2 states persistence more firmly than Table 1; no list of excluded studies; several citations are misplaced (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable; the sample sizes of the included studies are not given in the main text.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 105 studies from 2004-2015, synthesised qualitatively, the authors rate the evidence of impairment as strong and largely consistent for verbal learning and memory and for attention, both acutely and in people who use cannabis regularly; strong for acute psychomotor impairment; moderate for acute impairment of inhibition; and mixed, weak or absent for the other domains (Table 1). Persistence after abstinence is rated mixed for verbal learning and memory, working memory, attention, planning-type executive functions and verbal fluency, and weak for psychomotor function. It rests on 18 studies, most at 21-35 days of abstinence; 7 were prospective, and only 2 of those controlled for premorbid function (one found that adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls; the other an IQ decline that persisted after cessation or reduction). More than half of all studies did not report IQ or education, and many did not report or account for other substance use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that verbal learning and memory and attention "continue to be most consistently impaired by acute and chronic exposure to cannabis" and that these and some executive functions may persist after prolonged abstinence (AM p. 3); the Conclusions call it clear that impairment in a range of domains can persist beyond acute intoxication and may affect daily functioning and hence educational and psychosocial outcomes, especially in adolescents (AM p. 11). Gaps: (1) causal wording for chronic exposure, from mostly cross-sectional evidence that by the authors' own count is often unadjusted for premorbid ability, and the Dunedin cohort described as showing that cannabis use before 18 resulted in greater IQ decline (AM p. 10); (2) Table 2 calls persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function likely (AM p. 26), whereas Table 1 rates persistence as mixed for attention and weak for psychomotor function (AM pp. 24-25), and the Results suggest attentional impairment may reflect residual effects that fade as cannabinoids are cleared (AM p. 5); (3) prolonged abstinence mostly means 3 to 5 weeks; (4) the link to educational and psychosocial outcomes rests on one cited integrative cohort analysis (Silins et al., 2014) and lies outside the review, which excluded real-world tasks; (5) the ratings are the authors' subjective consensus. Against this, the Discussion says recovery remains contentious, that verbal learning and memory may recover with prolonged abstinence, and that persistence or recovery across domains is under-researched.

timeline.event: Solowij (1995), ref. 141, an earlier study by the senior author: attentional processing deficits related to duration of use in people abstinent 2 years (cited in the Discussion).
Pope et al. (2001), ref. 134, cited with Schreiner & Dunn (2012) as previous findings consistent with recovery of verbal learning and memory.

Lyons et al. (2004), ref. 64, monozygotic twins discordant for use, abstinent more than 12 months: read by its authors as evidence against long-term effects; Broyd et al. point to the Block Design deficit and trends in delayed and cued recall and finger tapping in the twins who had used.
Fried et al. (2005), ref. 79, prospective with testing before use: adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls on any cognitive measure.
Tait et al. (2011), ref. 66, 8-year cohort assessed three times: people who had stopped heavy use for at least 12 months did not differ from people who had not used cannabis on any cognitive measure.
Meier et al. (2012), ref. 60, Dunedin: IQ decline of about 6 points with persistent use or dependence, not restored by cessation in adolescent-onset use (as described here).

Schreiner & Dunn (2012), ref. 135, meta-analysis of residual effects on neurocognitive performance after prolonged abstinence: cited only as a previous finding, although the review states that no systematic review of task-based measures existed.
Rogeberg (2013), critique of the Dunedin IQ analysis (socioeconomic confounding), and the reply by Moffitt et al. (2013): both in the project's Tier A list; not discussed by this review.
Bosker et al. (2013), ref. 91: adults who used cannabis daily improved on critical tracking and divided attention over 8-23 days of abstinence but remained impaired against controls.
Narrative review published the same year states that cognitive impairments do not persist beyond 4-6 weeks of abstinence, citing Pope et al. (2001) and Schreiner & Dunn (2012)

Later tests in the project's Tier A list post-date the search: the UK and US IQ cohorts (Mokrysz et al., 2016; Jackson et al., 2016), a co-twin control study (Meier et al., 2018) and a meta-analysis of adolescents and young adults (Scott et al., 2018).

replication.where_it_stands: A systematic listing of the 2004-2015 task-based literature, useful for which domains were studied and which were found impaired in acute, chronic and abstinence studies, but without pooling, without study-level appraisal and with persistence judged from 18 studies, mostly at 3 to 5 weeks. Its ratings are the authors' consensus. Claims on lasting effects should rest on the primary prospective and co-twin studies it describes (Fried et al., 2005; Meier et al., 2012; Tait et al., 2011; Lyons et al., 2004) and on the later tests in the project's Tier A list, not on its ratings alone; the Dunedin figure should be taken from Meier et al. (2012), since this review and Curran et al. (2016) report it differently.

funding.funder: Australian Research Council (FT110100752 to NS) and National Health and Medical Research Council (Project Grant 1007593 to NS; Senior Research Fellowship 1021973 to MY) (Acknowledgments, AM p. 11). A research assistant is thanked for help with literature searches and document retrieval.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors report no biomedical financial interests or potential conflicts of interest (Financial disclosures, AM p. 12).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Wollongong and Illawarra Health and Medical Research Institute (Broyd, van Hell, Beale, Solowij); Monash University (Yücel). Broyd, van Hell and Solowij are stated to have contributed equally. Two included studies (refs 47, 124) and several background reviews and the earlier abstinence study (refs 18-21, 141) are by the senior author; no procedure for appraising the authors' own studies is described. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A registered systematic review with meta-analysis of cognitive outcomes stratified by verified abstinence duration (days, weeks, months, years), with study-level risk of bias and adjustment for premorbid ability and other substance use; and prospective cohorts that test cognition before first use and repeatedly through biologically verified sustained abstinence, with co-twin comparisons.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, exposure (acute administration or regular or former use) and outcomes (task performance) are specified, but no comparator is (Figure 1 legend, AM p. 23); within-group associations with use metrics were also eligible (Method, AM p. 4). A close call; not a critical item.
No protocol, registration or a priori plan is mentioned; the review says only that it followed the PRISMA reporting guideline (Method, AM p. 4).

Acute administration studies, cross-sectional comparisons and prospective studies were all eligible (case studies excluded), without an explanation of the choice, and they are synthesised together within each domain.

Two databases (PubMed, Scopus) with the strategy in Supplement 1 (not read); a date limit of January 2004 to February 2015 framed as the past decade, with no reason given for excluding earlier studies; language limits not stated in the main text; no reference-list, registry, grey-literature or expert searching reported; search completed within 24 months of acceptance. Judged as AMSTAR 2 item 4 is written (strict reading, decision p-amstar2-item4); a lenient reading that accepted the date window as a scope decision would give partial yes. The overall rating does not turn on it.
The main text does not say who screened titles or full texts; the search is described in Supplement 1 (not read).
The items extracted are listed (Method, AM p. 4) and the extraction is said to be detailed in Supplement 1 (not read); who extracted is not stated in the main text.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives 260 full-text exclusions without reasons (AM p. 27), and the paper does not say that a list of excluded studies exists in the supplements.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The main text gives no per-study description (Table 1 lists only reference numbers by domain); per-study demographics, use metrics, abstinence, other substance use, doses, tasks and findings are said to be tabulated in Supplement 2, Table S1 (not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool was used and no study-level appraisal is reported. Study quality (design, sample size) entered the Table 1 ratings only as a subjective consensus weighting (Table 1 footnote, AM p. 25); the Discussion reports confounding across the literature in aggregate (more than 50% of studies without IQ or education; other substance use often unreported) but not which studies were affected (AM p. 9).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported; funding is not among the extracted items (Method, AM p. 4).
Qualitative synthesis only; no reason for not pooling is stated beyond the heterogeneity of tasks and samples discussed (AM p. 8).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion has a section on confounding (premorbid functioning, other substance use), names the prospective design with pre-use testing as the strongest, reports where IQ-matched or IQ-adjusted studies did and did not find persistent impairment (AM p. 9) and notes that two prospective abstinence studies were confounded by concurrent treatment (AM p. 10). Judged met on balance, a close call: the Conclusions (AM p. 11) and Table 2 (AM p. 26) do not carry these limits through.

Mixed findings are attributed to heterogeneity in tasks, extent of exposure, use metrics, route and dose, tolerance and neurodevelopmental stage (AM pp. 8, 11), and one explanation is examined descriptively (executive deficits found mainly in older samples, AM p. 6); the explanations are post hoc.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a statement of no conflicts are given (AM pp. 11-12); that two included studies are the senior author's is not flagged.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 5, 6 and 8 can be judged only from Supplements 1 and 2, which were not read; none of them is a critical item, so the overall rating cannot change on them. Four critical items fail: no protocol (item 2), a restricted and partly undocumented search (item 4), no list of excluded studies (item 7) and no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies (item 9); items 11 and 15 do not apply because nothing was pooled, and item 13 is met on balance. With more than one critical flaw, AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. This rates the review's conduct, not the importance of its question: it is a useful map of which domains 2004-2015 studies examined and found impaired in acute, chronic and abstinence designs, and of how few studies addressed recovery. Its ratings are the authors' consensus, not graded evidence, and its statements on persistence rest on 18 studies mostly at 3 to 5 weeks of abstinence; claims about lasting effects should be traced to the primary studies it names. Version read: the accepted manuscript.

key_findings.finding: Scope and search: a systematic review, reported to PRISMA, of empirical studies published January 2004 to February 2015 on acute and chronic effects of cannabis and cannabinoids on neuropsychological task performance and on persistence or recovery after abstinence. Records identified: 3,021 in PubMed and 3,220 in Scopus; 316 and 225 kept after title assessment; 356 after removal of duplicates, all screened in full text; 260 excluded; 105 studies included in a qualitative synthesis. The search strategy and data extraction are described in Supplement 1 and per-study data in Supplement 2, Table S1 (neither on file). The introduction puts people using cannabis at 178 million (as cited: AIHW, 2013; UNODC, 2014; Volkow et al., 2014) and states that no systematic review of task-based measures of cognition had been done.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (AM p. 2); Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (AM p. 3); Method, paragraph (AM p. 4); Figure 1 (AM p. 27)
key_findings.note: Accepted manuscript; AM page numbers are PDF pages (the manuscript's own footer numbers run one lower). The PRISMA counts do not add up (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Eligibility: neuropsychological or cognitive experimental tasks given to people with regular or former cannabis use or after acute administration of cannabis or synthetic or plant cannabinoids, in humans, with cannabis the primary drug. Excluded: other primary drugs; questionnaire (trait) measures of cognition; samples with major psychopathology or neurological conditions; animal studies; neuroimaging, electrophysiological or autonomic primary outcomes; treatment as the primary focus; real-world multiplex tasks such as driving; case studies.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Strength ratings (acute / chronic / persistence with abstinence): verbal learning and memory +++ / +++ / +-; working memory +- / +- / +-; other memory functions + / +- / -; attention +++ / +++ / +-; attentional bias + / +++ / not investigated; psychomotor function +++ / + / +; planning, reasoning, interference control and problem solving +- / +- / +-; inhibition ++ / +- / not investigated; verbal fluency - / +- / +-; time estimation +- / - / -; decision making +- / +- / -. Key: +++ strong and largely consistent evidence for impairment; ++ moderate; + weak, based on few studies; +- mixed; - little or no evidence.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rating columns and key
key_findings.note: The footnote says the ratings are a qualitative interpretation, subjectively weighed on the number and quality (design, sample size) of studies and reached by consensus of the review's authors; they are not graded or pooled evidence.

key_findings.finding: Numbers of studies per domain (acute / chronic / abstinence): verbal learning and memory 11 / 20 / 9; working memory 20 / 16 / 7; other memory functions 2 / 8 / 4; attention 16 / 14 / 10; attentional bias 1 / 7 / none; psychomotor function 18 / 10 / 6; planning, reasoning, interference control and problem solving 12 / 23 / 9; inhibition 5 / 9 / none; verbal fluency 3 / 6 / 4; time estimation 6 / 1 / 1; decision making 7 / 17 / 3. Moderators listed for verbal learning and memory: frequency, lifetime use, duration, age of onset and gender; for attention: dose, age of onset, length of abstinence and withdrawal effects.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Number of studies and Pertinent cannabis use parameters columns
key_findings.note: The counts printed match the reference numbers listed in each cell (editors' check); a study can appear in several domains.

key_findings.finding: Verbal learning and memory (word-list tasks): acute intravenous THC, vaporised cannabis and oral nabilone impaired immediate and delayed recall and sometimes recognition; pre-dosing with CBD or more CBD in the cannabis may protect against some THC-induced deficits (two studies, refs 40 and 44). Impairment continues to be observed in adolescents and young adults who use cannabis regularly (with two young-adult studies finding none), even with occasional use in one study; poorer performance has been associated with frequency, quantity, duration and earlier onset of use; long-term use appears more affected than short-term; one study linked greater impairment to higher THC relative to CBD exposure; improvement or recovery with abstinence was seen in some studies or indices but not in others.
key_findings.locator: Results › Memory › Verbal learning and memory, paragraph (AM p. 4, continuing on p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Working memory: acute THC, dronabinol or nabilone affected working memory inconsistently across tasks. Chronic use was associated with impairment on immediate recall, verbal reasoning and verbal n-back tasks in young adults but not on spatial working memory or digit span, whereas spatial working memory was impaired in adolescents; in older adults two studies found no impairment, while recent or heavy use was associated with poorer performance on WAIS working-memory tasks. Impairment persisted for a few weeks in one cited study (ref. 65) but appears mostly to resolve with longer abstinence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Memory › Working memory, paragraph
key_findings.note: The citations for resolution with longer abstinence include a 2006 review of acute effects (ref. 35) and a study described on AM p. 10 as showing impaired working memory after 53 days (ref. 85); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Attention: acute exposure impaired focused, divided or sustained attention, often dose-dependently, with lesser impairment possibly reflecting tolerance in daily use. Many studies reported impaired sustained and divided attention, processing speed, rapid visual information processing, visual search, tracking, trail making and paced serial addition in adolescents and adults who use cannabis and in people abstinent up to several weeks; one adult sample abstinent twenty-three days remained impaired against controls despite improving, with poorer attention associated with younger age of onset (also in 30-day abstinent adolescents); but several studies found no difference from controls on broader attention measures in people who had stopped. The authors suggest attentional impairment may reflect residual effects that dissipate gradually as cannabinoids are cleared from the body.
key_findings.locator: Results › Attention, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Psychomotor function: in people with infrequent use, smoked or vaporised cannabis impaired critical tracking and affected reaction time and motor control dose-dependently; in heavy use, high-dose smoked cannabis increased collisions in a virtual maze task but did not affect critical tracking; oral (or intravenous) THC, nabilone or dronabinol impaired psychomotor function in seven of eight studies, as stated. Chronic effects were mixed: impaired in four studies, improved in one and unaffected in two. Psychomotor function was impaired after 23 to 35 days of abstinence (four studies) with a trend after 12 months for finger tapping (one twin study).
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychomotor function, paragraph
key_findings.note: Seven, not eight, studies are cited for the acute oral or intravenous statement (six positive, one negative; editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Executive function: acute THC impaired planning, reasoning, interference control or problem solving in six studies but not in three, equally across occasional, moderate and heavy use. For chronic use, eight case-control comparisons were null, while several found deficits with heavy use, in adolescents, with early but not late adult onset, in older people and with persistent use in a longitudinal study; deficits tended to appear in older samples, which the authors suggest may reflect effects becoming evident after frontal-lobe maturation, while noting that older people have also had more lifetime exposure. Three abstinence studies in younger samples found no group differences, whereas deficits persisted in people aged about 35-50 abstinent at least 28 days, and in 12-month abstinent people aged 38-51 Block Design was the only significant difference from their co-twins who had not used. Acute THC consistently increased stop-signal reaction time; chronic findings on inhibition and on verbal fluency are inconsistent.
key_findings.locator: Results › Executive function, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (AM pp. 6-7)

key_findings.finding: Decision making: acute THC altered sensitivity to reward and punishment and increased risk taking in people with infrequent use (one study) and regular use (three), but not in two other studies. Chronic findings are mixed: poorer decision making in six studies, no clear group differences in six. Behavioural risk taking was greater in adolescents abstinent a mean 53 days and was associated with prior exposure in people abstinent 25 days; one study found no delay-discounting differences between people currently using, people abstinent and controls (ref. 128, a study of current and former cannabis dependence by its title). The authors conclude that the extent to which effects persist in chronic or abstinent use remains unclear.
key_findings.locator: Results › Decision making, reward processing and delay discounting, paragraph (AM p. 7, continuing on p. 8)

key_findings.finding: About 75% of the studies reviewed had predominantly male samples; gender effects were tested in about 12% and very few were found. The authors note that associations with frequency of use are more likely to reflect residual acute or subchronic effects, associations with dose residual or cumulative effects, and associations with duration more persistent alterations.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Acute studies: 23 tested a single sample of controls or people with occasional or infrequent use, 11 a single sample of people with regular, frequent or daily use, and only 4 compared groups directly (2 people who use cannabis against controls; 2 frequent against infrequent use); those 4 found blunted impairment with regular or frequent use on critical tracking and divided attention (smoked cannabis) or on spatial working memory, verbal memory (inconsistently) and time estimation (intravenous THC). Most acute studies assessed cognition once, immediately or within two to three hours of dosing, so the duration of impairment was not studied. The authors conclude that research on tolerance has not advanced beyond limited earlier evidence and that impairment, though possibly blunted, persists in regular use across psychomotor function, attention and (inconsistently) memory, with potential real-world effects such as on driving (Hartman & Huestis, 2013).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Dose, route of administration and tolerance effects, paragraph (AM p. 8, continuing on p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Confounding: more than 50% of studies did not report IQ or years of education, and a substantial number did not control for premorbid functioning; a disconcerting number failed to report or account for alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use, handled otherwise by heterogeneous exclusion criteria, matching or covariates. The authors state that the impairing effects of chronic use mostly held after controlling for other substance use, but not in all studies (details in Supplement 1). Where groups were matched on IQ or IQ was controlled, persistent impairments were reported in three studies (refs 79, 39, 61) but not in two others (refs 84, 128).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Specificity to cannabis and potential confounds, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Ref. 39 is an acute intravenous THC study in healthy people by its title; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Strongest design, as named by the authors: a large prospective study controlling for ability before first use, education and other substance use. They describe one (Meier et al., 2012, ref. 60, Dunedin): persistent cannabis use or dependence was associated with an IQ decline of about 6 points from childhood to age 38, reflecting broad decline rather than one domain; cessation did not restore IQ in adolescent-onset use; recent cannabis use and persistent tobacco, alcohol or other drug use were ruled out as explanations. Two further studies controlling for premorbid function found impaired verbal learning and memory in adolescents who use cannabis (Solowij et al., 2011, ref. 47, the senior author's study) and impaired immediate and delayed memory and processing speed in adolescents currently using, with those who had stopped no different from controls (Fried et al., 2005, ref. 79).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Specificity to cannabis and potential confounds, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand. On AM p. 10 the same study is described as showing that cannabis use before 18 resulted in greater IQ decline by 38, persisting after cessation or reduction of use in the past year: a different exposure definition and causal wording. Curran et al. (2016) give up to 6 IQ points (Box 1) and around 8 (text); take the figure from Meier et al. (2012).

key_findings.finding: Abstinence studies: 18 studies examined persistence or recovery after more than 24 hours of abstinence, most often several weeks (21-35 days), with only a few going beyond this. Eleven were cross-sectional comparisons of people who had stopped (abstinent 7 days to more than 1 year) with people still using and/or controls, 9 of them in adolescents or young adults; 7 were prospective, assessing people at baseline and follow-up over 21 days to 4-8 years of abstinence, and 2 of these were confounded by concurrent pharmacological treatment.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cross-sectional abstinence findings: persistent effects on some aspects of attention, verbal and working memory and psychomotor speed in adolescents abstinent 28 days (Medina et al., 2007, ref. 65) and 35 days (Winward et al., 2014, ref. 67), but not on other aspects or domains; poor performance was associated with lifetime exposure (ref. 65) and, in 30-day abstinent adolescents, with earlier onset, and it predicted relapse over one year (Hooper et al., 2014, ref. 95); impaired working memory and risk taking after 53 days (Hanson et al., 2014, ref. 85); poorer verbal fluency in young adults abstinent up to 4 weeks (McHale & Hunt, 2008, ref. 119); impaired executive function and information processing but not attention or working memory in older adults abstinent more than 28 days (Thames et al., 2014, ref. 57). In monozygotic twins discordant for use, abstinent more than 12 months (Lyons et al., 2004, ref. 64), the twins who had used performed worse on Block Design, with trends on long-delay and cued recall and finger tapping; Lyons et al. read their study as evidence against long-term effects, a reading Broyd et al. dispute.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Prospective studies: only two controlled for premorbid function; in one, adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls on any cognitive measure (Fried et al., 2005, ref. 79); in the other, cannabis use before 18 was followed by greater IQ decline by 38 that persisted after cessation or reduction in the past year (Meier et al., 2012, ref. 60). Poor verbal learning improved in adolescents by 2 weeks of abstinence, but visual search remained impaired at 3 weeks relative to baseline (Hanson et al., 2010, ref. 55); an adult sample improved on critical tracking and divided attention over 8-23 days but remained impaired against controls (Bosker et al., 2013, ref. 91); in a cohort assessed three times 4 years apart, people who had stopped heavy use for at least 12 months improved relative to people continuing heavy use on immediate verbal memory and did not differ from people who had not used cannabis on any cognitive measure (Tait et al., 2011, ref. 66).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' reading of persistence: recovery after prolonged abstinence remains contentious; some but not all recent studies, consistent with earlier findings (Pope et al., 2001; Schreiner & Dunn, 2012), suggest verbal learning and memory impairment may recover with prolonged abstinence, yet evidence of persistent dysfunction continues to emerge; the use metrics and neural mechanisms behind persistence are unknown; an earlier study by the senior author found attentional processing deficits related to duration of use in people abstinent 2 years (Solowij, 1995, ref. 141). They call for well-controlled prospective studies from current use through prolonged abstinence.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 1st paragraph (AM p. 10) and 4th paragraph (AM p. 10, continuing on p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions and Table 2: further significant evidence supports acute and chronic exposure to cannabinoids impairing cognition, especially verbal learning, memory and attention; mixed evidence in other domains is attributed to heterogeneity of tasks, use histories and metrics and neurodevelopmental stage; the authors call it clear that impairment in a range of domains can persist beyond acute intoxication and may affect daily functioning and hence educational and psychosocial outcomes, especially in adolescents (citing Silins et al., 2014); evidence that CBD protects against harms is growing but not definitive. Table 2 lists, for recovery with abstinence, likely persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function, possible persistent effects on verbal learning and memory, and insufficient and mixed evidence; for acute effects it lists impaired working memory and other memory functions.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, paragraph (AM p. 11); Table 2 (AM p. 26)
key_findings.note: Table 2 is stronger than Table 1 on persistence and on acute working memory; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Funding: Australian Research Council and National Health and Medical Research Council; all authors report no biomedical financial interests or potential conflicts of interest.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgments (AM p. 11); Financial disclosures (AM p. 12)

reporting_issues.issue: The PRISMA flow does not add up: 356 full-text records were screened and 260 excluded, which leaves 96, but 105 studies are shown as included; no reasons are given for the exclusions and no other source of records is shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Nine included studies (editors' arithmetic) have no traceable route into the review; the selection cannot be audited from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists 101 distinct studies across all its cells (editors' count of reference numbers 36-58, 60-128 and 142-150) against 105 stated as included, and its abstinence columns list 17 distinct studies against the 18 abstinence studies counted in the Discussion; the acute columns list 40 distinct studies against the 38 (23 + 11 + 4) counted in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The counts cannot be reconciled from the main text; the full list is presumably in Supplement 2 (not read). Minor for claims, which should cite study counts as printed with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 states likely persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function after abstinence and lists impaired working memory among acute effects, whereas Table 1 rates persistence as mixed (+-) for attention and weak (+) for psychomotor function, and acute working memory as mixed (+-), and the Results describe acute working-memory effects as inconsistent and attentional impairment as possibly residual and fading as cannabinoids are cleared.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary table is stronger than the review's own ratings and text; claims on persistence should use Table 1 and the text, not Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: Misplaced citations in the working-memory and confounding passages: among the studies cited for working memory resolving with longer abstinence are a 2006 review of acute effects on memory (ref. 35), a study that the Discussion describes as showing impaired working memory after 53 days of abstinence (ref. 85) and one it cites for persisting working-memory deficits in adolescents abstinent 35 days (ref. 67, Winward et al., 2014); among the studies cited for persistent impairment where IQ was matched or controlled is an acute intravenous THC study in healthy people (ref. 39, by its title).
reporting_issues.consequence: The support for both statements is weaker than the citation lists suggest; the primary studies must be checked before either statement is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The acute statement that oral (or intravenous) THC, nabilone or dronabinol impaired psychomotor function in seven of eight studies cites seven studies, six positive and one negative; and the acute working-memory cell of Table 1 includes, through the range 68-78, ref. 78, which by its title is a study of long-term heavy use rather than acute administration.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the study counts behind individual statements are not exact.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and introduction state that no systematic review of neuropsychological task-based measures had been conducted, but the reference list includes a 2012 meta-analysis of residual effects of cannabis on neurocognitive performance after prolonged abstinence (Schreiner & Dunn, 2012, ref. 135), cited only as a previous finding.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review was not the first systematic synthesis of task-based outcomes after abstinence; its relation to the earlier meta-analysis (overlap, agreement) is not discussed.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 3 (Volkow et al., 2014, Adverse health effects of marijuana use) is given as N Engl J Med 371:879 with three authors, whereas Curran et al. (2016, ref. 3) cite the same title as N Engl J Med 370:2219-2227 with four authors.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the citation in this review may point to a correction or letter rather than the article; use the DOI when building the reference for that paper.
